I'm from Czech Republic. We have a representative (parliamentary) democracy as well, but there are a few differences.

Firstly, we have lots of political parties. Until not long ago, there used to be two major parties (ČSSD – Czech Socially-Democratic party, left-leaning, vs ODS – Citizens' Democratic Party, right-leaning) one of which usually won over half or almost half of the votes and created a coalition with other similarly leaning parties. Lately though the waters have been stirring. ODS has had lots of corruption scandals and their votes no longer trust them and have been scattering the votes among other parties, notably TOP09 – which is even more right-leaning than ODS. ČSSD has had their fair share of scandals as well though, so its position has also weakened, which has left the two parties' unshakeable positions as the political evergreens threatened and voters are looking for alternatives.

The latest elections were won by ČSSD and ANO. The latter is a slightly left-leaning political party led by Andrej Babiš, who is pretty much an oligarch, he owns lots of corporations and even most of the media, so you can imagine his power and influence. He had the money to pay for a big promotion before the elections and was voted into the parliament, because he said what people wanted to hear.

But I digress. TL;DR: The main difference of Czech politics vs. the US politics is that if you vote for a different party than the two major players, your vote does not go down the drain. Any party, no matter how new, has a chance to get in power.

Australian checking in.

We have three levels of government: Federal, State and Local.

Federal has two houses (Lower House = House of Representatives; Upper House = Senate), we elect both democratically with preferential voting. Lower house has a term of about 3 years and the upper house has a term of about 6 years (I think), but half of the upper house is re-elected each time (i.e. alternating). Parties can form coalitions (voting blocks); the group with the majority in the lower house forms government (nominates the Prime Minister). Bills are proposed by the lower house; once voted on and passed (by simple majority I think), they are voted on by the upper house; if passed, they are then rubber stamped by the Governor General who is a proxy for the Queen (the Governor General is appointed by the government).

State government works the same way, but has different names for the houses and doesn't have a Govern General figure. We also vote in the local governments (Councils), but honestly I've never looked into how that works. Federal, State and Local each have different scopes/powers (i.e. some laws are at a federal level, others are state-by-state). All taxation is federal (I believe), and they allocate money to the states by agreement. Some levies are on a state-by-state basis (e.g. registration of vehicles, stamp duty, possibly land tax), and some are at a council level (e.g. rates). Beyond that there are a lot of technicalities that I won't bore anyone with. I may be wrong about some of this - feel free to correct me.
